# Diagnosing HVAC Air Routing Issues on a 1995 Chevy S-10 Blazer

When an HVAC system suddenly routes all airflow to the defroster and floor vents regardless of selector position, it often signals a catastrophic failure in the vacuum logic or a mechanical blockage. In this case, we are dealing with a 1995 Chevy S-10 Blazer equipped with the 4.3L Vortec V6 (VIN W) and PCM. The vehicle has accumulated 230,000 miles on its original engine.

The symptom appeared immediately after replacing the Idle Air Control (IAC) valve. The owner changed the IAC, and coincidentally, the HVAC behavior shifted from normal operation to blowing exclusively through the defroster and floor in all modes: AC, Heat, Vent, etc. Since the old IAC was reinstalled and the issue persisted, the correlation was dismissed as a coincidence. Further checks confirmed engine vacuum levels were stable, with no leaks detected at the intake manifold or via carb cleaner tests. The engine even ran smoother post-replacement, suggesting the IAC swap did not introduce new vacuum leaks in the engine bay.

However, the root cause lies in the HVAC control system's ability to actuate doors based on vacuum pressure. The owner noted a history of intermittent issues previously solved by replacing the HVAC control switch. In this specific instance, a genuine AC/Delco switch had been installed just two months prior and was functioning perfectly until the IAC replacement event.

Upon removing the dash panel, a distinct hissing sound emanated from the HVAC control switch area. Initial diagnostics involved unplugging the vacuum line assembly to measure source pressure directly against engine vacuum; this confirmed the upstream supply was intact. The next step involved manually applying vacuum via a pump while following the schematic. This bypass test revealed that the actuators themselves were functional, as they could move the doors independently (heater, defroster, and vents) when supplied with manual vacuum.

The diagnostic pivot occurred when reconnecting the lines to the switch. While holding the connector on the switch in a specific orientation, the system temporarily behaved correctly, routing air to the Bi-level A/C, defroster, and heater as intended. This indicated that the leak was dynamic, changing based on the physical play within the stacked sections of the switch assembly or the rubber connector interface.

Using a homemade stethoscope made from tubing, the final diagnosis pinpointed the vacuum leak originating internally from the "new" HVAC control switch itself. Despite being installed only two months ago, the unit failed to maintain vacuum integrity under load, causing the system to default to a specific actuator position or fail to engage the others, resulting in air blowing out of the defroster and floor simultaneously.

This scenario highlights a critical trade-off in automotive repair: assuming a component is fine because it was recently installed can be misleading if the installation environment changed or if the part had latent defects. The difficulty here stemmed from the mechanical play within the switch's clipped sections, making it hard to distinguish between a failing internal diaphragm and a compromised rubber connector assembly.

If you encounter similar routing issues, always isolate the vacuum supply from the control logic. If manual vacuum application works but system vacuum fails, the culprit is almost certainly an actuator or a leak in the switch assembly rather than the engine vacuum source. Given the age of the vehicle, sourcing a replacement HVAC switch that hasn't been refurbished with worn internals might be difficult; sometimes replacing the entire stack including the connector assembly yields better long-term reliability than swapping just the electronic faceplate.
